title: Tetralogy of Fallot
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Tetralogy of Fallot is a cyanotic congenital heart defect with a ventricular septal defect, pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy. It presents with cyanotic spells, a harsh systolic ejection murmur and clubbing. Management centres on surgical repair, with supportive care for hypoxaemia.

sections.p: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is a combination of four cardiac anomalies that cause right‑to‑left shunting and cyanosis. Diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by echocardiography. In low‑resource settings, a focused bedside echo or a portable handheld device can suffice.
b: Cyanosis, especially during crying or exertion
Harsh systolic ejection murmur at left upper sternal border
Digital clubbing
Tet spells (paroxysmal cyanosis relieved by squatting)

t.b: Shows VSD, pulmonary infundibular stenosis, overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy – confirms TOF
SpO2 <90% on room air, improves with squatting or handgrip
Boot‑shaped heart, prominent pulmonary arteries – supportive but not diagnostic

sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of pulmonary stenosis and cyanosis. The most widely used system is the Ross classification: Stage I (mild), II (moderate), III (severe).
b: Stage I – mild infundibular stenosis, SpO2 90–95%
Stage II – moderate, SpO2 80–90%
Stage III – severe, SpO2 <80% or frequent spells

sections.p: TOF is a sporadic developmental defect of the outflow tract. In low‑resource settings, maternal infections (rubella, HIV), malnutrition, and teratogenic exposures (alcohol, certain herbal remedies) are considered risk factors.
b: Genetic mutations (e.g., NKX2‑5, NOTCH1) – rare
Maternal rubella infection – uncommon in vaccinated populations
Maternal HIV – possible immunological effect
Malnutrition – zinc or folate deficiency

sections.p: Classic presentation is a young child with cyanosis, especially during crying or exertion, a harsh systolic murmur, and clubbing. Tet spells are episodic cyanosis relieved by squatting.
b: Cyanosis at rest or with activity
Harsh systolic ejection murmur
Digital clubbing
Tet spells – sudden cyanosis, pallor, tachycardia

sections.p: Investigation priorities are rapid, bedside‑friendly tests. When advanced imaging is unavailable, clinical assessment and basic labs guide management.

t.b: Normal heart size and pulmonary vasculature

sections.p: Urgent red flags include severe hypoxaemia, heart failure, arrhythmias, and infection. Complications can be acute (tet spells, heart failure) or chronic (pulmonary hypertension, arrhythmia).
b: SpO2 <70% or worsening despite squatting
Rapidly increasing cyanosis
Signs of heart failure – tachypnoea, hepatomegaly

sections.p: Management is staged: initial stabilization, then definitive surgical repair. Supportive care focuses on oxygenation, fluid balance and infection prevention.
b: Oxygen therapy – 2–4 L/min via nasal cannula or face mask

t.b: Avoid if ductus is already closed

sections.p: Post‑repair follow‑up includes monitoring for residual shunt, arrhythmia and pulmonary hypertension. Prevention focuses on maternal health and vaccination.
b: Regular ECG and echo at 6 months, 1 year, then annually

sections.p: Conditions that mimic TOF include other cyanotic CHDs (e.g., transposition of the great arteries), severe asthma, and severe anemia.
b: Transposition of the great arteries – harsh systolic murmur, cyanosis but no pulmonary stenosis

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, a normal chest X‑ray can miss TOF; a normal SpO2 on rest may be misleading if the child is not exerted.
b: SpO2 may be >90% at rest but drop during activity

t.b: An episode of sudden cyanosis, pallor and tachycardia, relieved by squatting or handgrip.
Increases systemic vascular resistance, reducing right‑to‑left shunt and improving oxygenation.
All patients with moderate to severe TOF; early repair reduces mortality and improves growth.

faq.a: An acute cyanotic episode relieved by squatting or handgrip.
It increases systemic vascular resistance, reducing the right‑to‑left shunt.
All patients with moderate to severe TOF; early repair improves outcomes.

exam: What is the most likely cause of a 2‑year‑old with cyanosis, a harsh systolic murmur and clubbing? — VSD with pulmonary stenosis (Tetralogy of Fallot).
During a tet spell, which manoeuvre is most effective? — Squatting or handgrip to increase SVR.
A child with TOF presents with SpO2 78% on room air. What is the next step? — Start oxygen therapy and arrange urgent echo.
What is the key echocardiographic finding in TOF? — VSD, overriding aorta, pulmonary infundibular stenosis and RV hypertrophy.
Why is prostaglandin E1 used in severe TOF? — To keep the ductus arteriosus open and maintain systemic flow.
Which complication is most common after TOF repair? — Pulmonary regurgitation leading to RV dilation.
